title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing
summary: Explore sleep rhythms, common sleep difficulties, realistic routines, and when professional assessment matters.

UNDERSTANDING SLEEP AND MENTAL WELLBEING
Mental Health Educational Content Library | Expanded Chapter 08
Purpose. To help readers understand sleep physiology, recognize common sleep problems, develop supportive routines, and know when professional medical or psychological care is needed.
Audience. General adult readers, older adolescents with appropriate support, caregivers, educators, and community health educators.

Publication status. Evidence-informed educational draft. This handbook is not a diagnostic tool or a substitute for individualized professional care. Clinical review, Rwanda-specific referral checks, accessibility review, and human-reviewed translation are required before public release.
Edition 1.0 | 11 November 2026 | English

Important: If you are extremely sleepy, avoid driving or operating machinery. If you have severe difficulty breathing during sleep, sudden loss of consciousness, or other acute symptoms, seek appropriate medical care.
Learning goals and chapter map

After this chapter, a learner should be able to describe the main stages and regulators of sleep, recognize common patterns of sleep difficulty, explain the relationship between sleep and emotional wellbeing, identify supportive daily habits, and seek appropriate professional assessment when needed.

sections.title: What is sleep, and why do we need it?

blocks.text: Sleep is a natural, recurring state in which the brain and body undergo coordinated changes. It is not simply a period of inactivity. During sleep, the brain cycles through different stages that support attention, learning, memory, emotional processing and physical functioning. The value of sleep is not measured by duration alone: timing, continuity and how rested a person feels during the day also matter. [1-3]

A single difficult night is common and does not necessarily indicate a disorder. Sleep becomes a greater concern when problems persist, are distressing, or interfere with safe and effective daily life. A person with adequate time in bed may still get poor-quality sleep because of repeated awakenings or an underlying disorder.
Why the topic belongs in mental health education

Sleep and mental health affect each other. Stress, anxiety, depression, trauma-related symptoms and other difficulties may interfere with sleep. Repeated poor sleep can also worsen concentration, irritability, emotional regulation and coping capacity. This does not mean that every person who sleeps poorly has a mental illness. [3,4]

The circadian rhythm is an approximately 24-hour timing system that influences when we feel alert, sleepy, hungry and ready for activity. Light, daily activity and regular waking patterns help synchronize it. The brain receives information about environmental light and uses it to coordinate the sleep-wake cycle. The hormone melatonin typically rises as darkness approaches, helping signal nighttime. [2]

For example, a student who stays awake on a phone until very late and sleeps until noon on weekends may find it difficult to become sleepy at an earlier school-night bedtime. However, teenagers naturally tend toward later sleep timing than younger children; this biological shift should not be mistaken for laziness.
Sleep pressure

A second process is the drive to sleep that builds while we are awake. Sleep pressure generally increases as waking hours pass and decreases during sleep. Together, sleep pressure and the circadian rhythm influence when we fall asleep and wake up. Caffeine can temporarily reduce our sense of sleepiness but does not replace the restorative functions of sleep. [2]
Typical sleep contains both non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) and rapid-eye-movement (REM) stages, cycling several times. Patterns change with age and across the night. [5]

rows: A light transition from wakefulness into sleep; easy to awaken.
More established sleep; body functions slow and external awareness decreases.
Deep or slow-wave sleep; especially prominent earlier in the night.
Brain activity changes; vivid dreams are common and memory/emotional functions are supported.

blocks.text: No single stage is the only "important" stage. Normal sleep includes a balance across stages, and consumer sleep trackers cannot reliably diagnose a sleep disorder based solely on their stage estimates.

sections.title: How much sleep is generally recommended?

blocks.text: Recommended sleep amounts depend on age, and they describe population guidance rather than a rigid score for each individual. Some people need more sleep when ill or recovering from lost sleep. [1,6]

A person who works long shifts, shares a crowded home, experiences nighttime noise, or cares for a young child may have limited control over sleep time. Educational advice must acknowledge these real barriers instead of blaming the individual.

sections.title: What is insufficient or poor-quality sleep?

blocks.text: Insufficient sleep means obtaining less sleep than the body needs. Sleep deficiency can also involve poor timing, interrupted sleep, or a condition that reduces restorative sleep. Possible daytime consequences include low alertness, difficulty remembering information, slower reaction time, changes in mood and greater risk during driving or hazardous tasks. [3]
Common signs worth noticing

items: Frequently feeling sleepy or unintentionally dozing during the day.
Struggling to concentrate at school, work or during conversations.
Needing much more time than usual to complete simple tasks.
Becoming more irritable or emotionally reactive after poor nights.
Feeling unrefreshed despite giving yourself adequate opportunity to sleep.

blocks.text: Symptoms can also arise from anemia, medication side effects, other illnesses, depression or other conditions. A professional assessment can help determine the cause.

sections.title: Insomnia: more than one bad night

blocks.text: Insomnia involves difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or returning to sleep after waking, despite an adequate opportunity to sleep, with associated distress or daytime impairment. Temporary insomnia may follow stress, illness, travel, grief or major changes. Chronic insomnia is a more persistent clinical pattern and should not be diagnosed from a simple website checklist. [7-9]
Common maintaining patterns

A person who worries about whether they will sleep may become increasingly alert at bedtime. Spending extra hours awake in bed, monitoring the clock, or irregular sleep timing can sometimes maintain the problem. Persistent insomnia may also coexist with pain, anxiety, depression, substance use or other sleep disorders.

Example: A university student spends several nights awake before examinations. After the examination ends, the student keeps worrying about sleep and begins staying in bed much longer to "catch up." The difficulty continues. A clinician can assess whether insomnia-focused treatment is appropriate.

sections.title: Other sleep conditions people should know about

blocks.text: Obstructive sleep apnea

Sleep apnea may involve repeated breathing interruptions, loud snoring, gasping or choking during sleep, and daytime sleepiness. Not everyone with sleep apnea snores. People with these symptoms should seek medical assessment; sleep hygiene alone cannot treat the underlying breathing disorder.
Circadian rhythm sleep-wake difficulties

Some people cannot align their natural sleep timing with work, school or social schedules. Shift work, jet lag and delayed sleep timing may contribute. Treatment depends on the pattern and may require specialist guidance.
Restless legs, parasomnias and hypersomnolence

Uncomfortable sensations that improve with moving the legs, unusual behaviors during sleep, or severe daytime sleepiness deserve evaluation. Falling asleep unexpectedly or experiencing sleep attacks should not be assumed to result only from a busy schedule.

sections.title: How sleep and mental health interact

blocks.text: Stress and worry

When the body is on alert, it can be harder to settle at night. Sleep loss can make daily stressors feel harder to manage. Gentle routines may help, but people facing ongoing insecurity or hardship also need practical support.
Anxiety
Worry about future events or sleep itself may prolong wakefulness. Persistent sleep difficulties and anxiety symptoms should be assessed together rather than treated as unrelated issues.
Depression

Depression may be associated with difficulty sleeping, early waking or sleeping much longer than usual. Changes in sleep alone do not establish depression, and treatment decisions require careful assessment.
Trauma-related symptoms
Nightmares, hypervigilance or a feeling of unsafety may disrupt rest. Survivors should not be pressured to close their eyes, disclose memories, or perform relaxation exercises that increase distress.
Bipolar disorder

A markedly reduced need for sleep accompanied by unusually high energy, elevated or irritable mood, racing thoughts or impulsive behavior can be a warning sign that needs prompt professional assessment. This is different from ordinary insomnia accompanied by fatigue.

sections.title: Everyday habits that can support sleep

blocks.text: Healthy sleep routines are useful for general wellbeing and can complement clinical care. They are not, on their own, an adequate treatment for chronic insomnia disorder. [1,8-10]

items: Choose a wake-up time that is as consistent as your responsibilities allow.
Seek natural daylight and appropriate activity during the day.
Build a predictable winding-down routine: reading, quiet conversation, gentle music or another calming activity.
Reduce bright screen use close to bedtime if feasible, especially when it keeps you alert.
Limit caffeine in the afternoon and evening if it affects you.
Keep the sleep space as dark, quiet, comfortable and safe as reasonably possible.
Avoid using alcohol as a sleep aid: it can fragment sleep and has other risks.
If an environment is unsafe or crowded, focus on feasible improvements and seek practical support rather than blaming yourself.

sections.title: Practical barriers in Rwanda-relevant daily life

blocks.text: A reader may share one room with family members, work evening shifts, study under difficult conditions, manage caregiving duties or have limited privacy. Advice should prioritize realistic actions. For example, a household may coordinate a quieter period, reduce unnecessary night lighting, or plan a more reliable morning routine when possible. These are illustrative situations, not claims about all Rwandan households.

When poverty, housing insecurity, severe stress, violence or illness disrupt sleep, an individual routine cannot resolve the underlying problem. Health education should connect people to medical, social and practical support where appropriate.
What is CBT-I?

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured treatment that addresses sleep-related patterns of thinking and behavior. It can include education, tailored behavioral strategies, cognitive approaches and follow-up. Multiple clinical guidelines recommend multicomponent CBT-I as first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults. [8,9]

Specialist CBT-I may include methods such as sleep restriction or sleep compression. These should not be copied from a handout without assessment, especially for people with certain medical or psychiatric conditions, excessive daytime sleepiness, high-risk work, or complex sleep problems.
Medication and supplements

A clinician may consider medication depending on symptoms, age, other conditions, pregnancy status, interactions and treatment history. Sleeping pills can have side effects and may not address the underlying cause. Do not start, combine, stop or change prescribed medicines on the basis of this chapter. Melatonin is not a universal cure for insomnia and suitability varies. [7,10]

sections.title: When should someone seek professional help?

blocks.text: Consider an appointment with a qualified healthcare professional when sleep difficulty persists, significantly affects mood, concentration, study or work, or occurs alongside loud snoring, breathing interruptions, repeated nightmares, unusual movements, severe daytime sleepiness, chronic pain or symptoms of a mental health condition.

Urgent medical assessment is warranted if a person has severe or unusual breathing problems, episodes of losing consciousness, serious injury associated with sleepiness, or new concerning symptoms. If a person is dangerously sleepy, they should not drive or operate machinery. If there are thoughts of suicide or immediate danger, seek urgent emergency assistance through available local emergency services or the nearest emergency department.
Where symptoms suggest mania or a significantly reduced need for sleep with marked behavioral changes, seek prompt clinical assessment.
A secondary-school learner studies very late, uses a bright phone in bed and struggles to wake for class. The learner feels irritable and forgetful.
Reflection: What realistic changes to study timing and evening routine might help? How might teachers or caregivers support the learner?
A healthcare worker rotates between late and early shifts and becomes sleepy during travel. Family responsibilities limit recovery time.
Reflection: Which barriers require schedule or workplace support? Why is drowsy travel a safety concern?
An adult worries about falling asleep and checks the clock throughout the night. Sleep problems continue for weeks and affect work.
Reflection: What makes this different from a single sleepless night? Why might CBT-I assessment help?
A family notices that one adult snores loudly, sometimes gasps during sleep and remains very tired during the day.
Reflection: Why should this person seek medical assessment rather than only trying herbal tea or an earlier bedtime?

sections.title: Guided activity A - My seven-day sleep observation

blocks.text: For seven days, readers may record sleep patterns without trying to force a target. This exercise is for awareness, not diagnosis or clinical sleep restriction. Avoid recording sensitive details on devices that are shared or monitored.

After the week, consider whether patterns change with shift work, phone use, stress, noise, illness, caffeine or caregiving. Bring the notes to a clinician if a sleep problem is ongoing. If recording sleep increases anxiety, stop tracking.

sections.title: Guided activity B - A gentle evening routine

blocks.text: Choose one or two realistic steps, not a rigid checklist: (1) identify tomorrow's priority tasks earlier in the evening, (2) choose a quiet activity for the final part of the day, (3) adjust brightness or noise where feasible, and (4) allow yourself to rest without checking the clock repeatedly.
Reflection: Which step is feasible in your home? What barrier would require someone else's cooperation? A routine should be adapted to safety, disability, caregiving and work schedules.

sections.title: Guided activity C - Distinguishing a worry from a plan

blocks.text: Write down an ordinary concern earlier in the evening if doing so feels comfortable. Divide it into "something I can act on tomorrow" and "something I cannot solve tonight." Choose one practical next action for tomorrow. Do not use this exercise to dismiss real danger, pain or urgent needs.

Example: "I may be late for work" can become "I will prepare my bag and check my transport plan." If a concern involves an unsafe environment or a serious medical symptom, practical safety assistance takes priority over relaxation.

Circadian rhythm: An approximately 24-hour cycle regulating alertness and many bodily functions.
Sleep pressure: The biological tendency to become sleepier with time awake.
REM: A sleep phase associated with characteristic eye movements and often vivid dreams.
NREM: Non-rapid-eye-movement sleep, including lighter and deeper stages.
Insomnia: Difficulty sleeping despite an opportunity to sleep, causing distress or impairment.
CBT-I: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia, a structured evidence-based treatment.
Sleep apnea: A sleep-related breathing disorder that requires medical assessment.
Sleep hygiene: Daily routines and environmental practices that can support healthy sleep.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing
summary: Understand connection, loneliness, respectful boundaries, communication, and safe ways to seek support.
author: VUGA NDAKUMVA
frontMatter: MENTAL HEALTH LIBRARY / CHAPTER 09
Relationships, Social
Connection, and Mental
Wellbeing
A practical, evidence-informed learning chapter for individuals, families, students, and communities in Rwanda.
Document status

Version 1.0 | 11 November 2026 | English. This is public-facing educational draft content, not a clinical assessment or personal treatment plan. Professional clinical, safeguarding, accessibility, and Kinyarwanda/French reviews are pending.
Learning outcomes

Describe how relationships and social connection can affect mental wellbeing. Distinguish loneliness, social isolation, solitude, and supportive connection. Recognize respect, reciprocity, healthy boundaries, and concerning interpersonal patterns. Practice communication, conflict resolution, and safe help-seeking skills. Identify when loneliness or relationship stress warrants professional support.
How to use this chapter

Read the sections in order, or choose a topic relevant to your situation. All scenarios are fictional. Exercises are optional; skip any that feel unsafe, intrusive, or emotionally overwhelming. For children, tailor activities with appropriate adult or professional guidance. This chapter does not require disclosure of personal experiences.

sections.title: Why relationships matter for mental health

blocks.text: People develop and maintain wellbeing through many forms of connection: friendships, family ties, classmates, colleagues, neighbours, mentors, peers, and chosen communities. Supportive relationships may offer comfort during setbacks, practical assistance, recognition, shared enjoyment, and a sense of belonging. They are one among many influences on mental health, alongside biology, life experiences, economic security, and access to healthcare [1-3].

Social connection is not measured only by the number of people in someone’s contacts. A person may have many acquaintances but few relationships in which they feel safe and understood. Another person may have a small circle and feel well supported. Relationship quality, reliability, and personal choice matter.

Connection can protect wellbeing without guaranteeing that a person will never experience depression, anxiety, or another mental health condition. Similarly, being socially isolated does not prove someone has a disorder. [1-3]

sections.title: Understanding social connection, loneliness, isolation, and solitude

blocks.text: Social connection

Social connection describes the structure, functions, and quality of how people relate to others. Structure includes who is in a person’s network and how often they interact. Function includes the type of emotional or practical support exchanged. Quality concerns whether interactions feel supportive, trustworthy, strained, or harmful. This three-part explanation follows the WHO social-connection framework [1].
Loneliness

Loneliness is a distressing feeling that occurs when a person experiences a gap between the relationships they want and those they believe they have. A person can feel lonely in a crowded classroom, busy workplace, or household. Loneliness is not a character flaw or proof of unpopularity
Social isolation

Social isolation refers to having relatively few relationships, social roles, or interactions. It may result from geographic distance, disability-related barriers, bereavement, discrimination, relocation, low income, or other circumstances. Someone can be isolated without feeling lonely, although the two often overlap [1].
Solitude

Solitude is time spent alone, sometimes intentionally and comfortably. Quiet time for rest, prayer, creative work, or reflection can be valuable. Being alone is not automatically unhealthy. What matters is whether the person can access the level and quality of connection they need.
Reflection
Which word best describes your current experience: connected, lonely, isolated, enjoying solitude, or unsure? There is no right answer. You may experience more than one at the same time.

sections.title: Healthy relationships: what to look for

blocks.text: A healthy relationship is not a relationship without disagreements. It is one in which people can disagree, grow, and make choices while preserving one another’s dignity. Healthy relationships may include:

items: Respect: each person’s needs, privacy, identity, and decisions are taken seriously.
Trust: promises are generally kept; questions can be discussed without intimidation.
Mutuality: both parties have room to speak, give, receive, and make choices; equal contribution is not required every day.
Boundaries: people can say no, request time apart, and change their mind.
Support: care is offered without making the other person responsible for every emotion or problem.
Repair: after mistakes, people can acknowledge harm, take responsibility, and change behaviour.

blocks.text: Family, friendship, romantic, and professional relationships have different expectations. The same principle applies across them: caring for someone does not authorize monitoring, humiliating, isolating, or coercing them.

sections.title: Social support: emotional, practical, informational, and belonging

blocks.text: People need different kinds of support at different times. Emotional support involves empathy and being listened to. Practical support may include help with transportation, childcare, or sharing a task. Informational support involves reliable guidance or help finding services. Belonging comes from being part of a group in which a person feels accepted [2,3].

A student worried about examinations may benefit from a peer who listens, a tutor who helps organise revision, and a trusted adult who notices exhaustion. No single person has to meet all those needs. Developing more than one safe connection can reduce dependence on an individual relationship.
Offering support should not become pressure. Ask what someone wants before giving advice, involving others, or sharing a private situation.

sections.title: Why making and maintaining connections can be difficult

blocks.text: Challenges such as moving to a new district, unemployment, heavy school workloads, disability-related access barriers, caregiving, bereavement, social anxiety, experiences of discrimination, or limited money for transport can make maintaining relationships difficult. This is not evidence that a person is unwilling or incapable of friendship.

Some people also need more time alone than others. The goal is not to force sociability or make everyone attend large gatherings. It is to support meaningful relationships that fit individual preferences and safety.
When a person has been hurt or controlled in a relationship, rebuilding trust may require time and professional support. Encouraging immediate reconnection with unsafe individuals can increase risk.

Communication is not just about speaking clearly. It also involves checking what someone means, allowing silence, and noticing whether the conversation feels safe. Helpful skills can be practised gradually.
A four-step conversation method

items: Choose a suitable moment. Ask whether the other person has time and privacy to talk.
Describe what you observed without making an accusation: “I noticed we have barely spoken this week.”
Explain your feeling or need using “I” language: “I miss our conversations and would like to reconnect.”
Invite a response: “How has the week been for you?” Listen before deciding what to do next.

blocks.text: An “I” statement can make concerns easier to discuss, but it is not a guaranteed way to resolve conflict. If the other person threatens or intimidates you, communication techniques are not a substitute for safety planning.
Active listening

Active listening involves giving attention, avoiding unnecessary interruption, reflecting the meaning of what someone says, and asking permission before offering advice. A supportive reply may sound like: “That sounds exhausting. Would you prefer that I listen or help you think about options?”

Disagreements can arise from expectations, stress, financial strain, misunderstandings, or different priorities. Constructive conflict management includes slowing down, focusing on a specific issue, allowing each person a voice, agreeing on a realistic next step, and revisiting the matter when calm.

For instance, two housemates may disagree over shared chores. They could identify the tasks, discuss what each can realistically manage, write down a fair arrangement, and review it after a week. The goal is not winning an argument but developing a workable agreement.
Safety distinction

Ordinary disagreement is not the same as intimidation, coercive control, stalking, threats, or violence. If a person feels unsafe, avoid encouraging joint confrontation, mediation, or couples exercises as a default. Seek appropriate specialist assistance instead.

Boundaries are limits that protect time, privacy, emotional energy, and personal choices. A boundary is not a punishment; it describes what a person can accept and what they will do to care for themselves. Examples include choosing when to answer messages, deciding what information to share, asking before discussing a sensitive topic, and refusing to lend money one cannot afford to lose.
A respectful boundary might be: “I cannot talk about this during work. I can speak after 6 p.m.”

Another might be: “I am not ready to discuss that experience.” Setting a boundary does not guarantee another person will respect it. In unsafe relationships, personal safety should take priority over explaining a boundary repeatedly.

Emotional support does not mean becoming someone’s clinician, remaining available every hour, or keeping dangerous secrets. It is appropriate to seek extra help when a problem exceeds what a friend or family member can safely manage.

sections.title: Loneliness and its effects on wellbeing

blocks.text: Prolonged loneliness and isolation are associated with poorer mental and physical health, although the relationship is complex and not all individuals are affected in the same way [1-4]. Loneliness may involve sadness, restlessness, reduced motivation, difficulty trusting others, or the sense that one is disconnected even while surrounded by people.

Noticing loneliness can be a useful signal that a need for connection is unmet. It should not be treated as a diagnosis. A person whose loneliness occurs alongside persistent low mood, anxiety, sleep disturbance, or substantial impairment may benefit from professional assessment.
Gentle steps toward connection

items: Identify one person or community setting that has previously felt reasonably safe.
Choose a small action, such as a brief greeting, a message, or attending one group activity.
Prefer shared interests over pressure to disclose private feelings.
Repeat contact at a manageable pace; friendships often develop through time.
If a group does not feel welcoming or safe, it is acceptable to try another setting.

blocks.text: Messaging apps, online learning groups, and social platforms can help people stay connected across long distances. They can also create pressure to respond immediately, comparisons with others, misunderstandings, or exposure to harassment. The quality and safety of an interaction matter more than whether it happens online or in person.

Useful digital boundaries include asking before sharing someone else’s photo or story, respecting delayed replies, choosing privacy settings thoughtfully, and avoiding arguments in public comment sections when a private conversation would be safer. Digital access may not be private for someone whose device is monitored. If someone is being threatened or monitored, changing settings or blocking a contact might alert the person causing harm. Specialist digital safety support may be needed before taking action.

Families and caregivers can support wellbeing through reliable attention, predictable care, encouragement, and help during difficulties. Friends and peers may provide acceptance and shared experiences. Teachers, mentors, health workers, and community members may also become valuable sources of support.

However, not every family or community relationship is safe. People should not be encouraged to disclose private mental health concerns to relatives, religious leaders, or peers without considering trust, confidentiality, and personal choice.

For adolescents, safe relationships with trusted adults are important. Adults should listen respectfully, avoid dismissing concerns as “just a phase,” and seek appropriate professional or safeguarding assistance when serious risks arise [3,5].

In Rwanda, possible opportunities for social connection may include school clubs, youth groups, sports teams, community activities, volunteer initiatives, faith communities, study circles, neighbourhood associations, and peer-support programmes. These are illustrative settings, not guaranteed services or endorsements.

Participation should remain voluntary. Activities should be inclusive of people with disabilities, individuals living far from community centres, people with limited connectivity, and those who may not feel safe in some groups. Privacy and protection from stigma are especially important when mental health is discussed.
Community programmes can support connection by providing accessible meeting places, predictable schedules, welcoming facilitators, and a way to raise concerns safely [1,2].

sections.title: Supporting someone who feels lonely or distressed

blocks.text: Begin by asking how the person would like to be supported. Offer specific, practical options instead of making broad promises. For example: “Would you like me to check in this weekend?” or “Would it help to walk together after class?” Respect a no and avoid turning an invitation into pressure.

Do not assume that frequent contact is always best. Some people need time, rest, or privacy. If a person speaks about hopelessness, self-harm, or suicide, take it seriously and seek appropriate urgent professional support. Do not promise to keep an immediate safety risk secret.

Consider consultation with a qualified healthcare or mental health professional when loneliness, social withdrawal, or interpersonal stress becomes persistent, overwhelming, or interferes with sleep, school, employment, or daily responsibilities; when anxiety or depression symptoms are present; or when repeated conflict or trauma makes it difficult to feel safe.

Urgent assistance is needed when there is immediate danger, threats of serious violence, or concern that someone may act on thoughts of suicide or self-harm. Seek available emergency medical assistance or the nearest appropriate emergency facility. Specific Rwanda contacts and operating hours must be confirmed before publication of this chapter.

blocks.title: Scenario A — A first-year university student in Kigali

blocks.text: A student moved from Musanze for university. Although they speak with many classmates, they feel they have no one to rely on. They decide to attend a small study group twice and message a former school friend. Discussion: Why can someone be lonely around other people? What makes a manageable first step?

blocks.title: Scenario B — A parent balancing work and caregiving

blocks.text: A parent with long working hours has little opportunity to meet friends. Instead of committing to several activities, they arrange a short weekly call with a trusted person and ask whether a neighbour can occasionally help with a practical task. Discussion: What barriers make connection difficult? How can support include practical help?

One friend feels ignored when replies arrive late. The other explains they often share a phone and have limited data. They agree not to interpret slow replies as rejection and decide on a regular time to catch up. Discussion: How did assumptions influence the disagreement?

blocks.title: Scenario D — Pressure within a relationship

blocks.text: A person’s partner demands their phone password, discourages friendships, and becomes angry when they attend a community event. A trusted mentor suggests individual specialist support rather than an immediate confrontation. Discussion: Which behaviours go beyond ordinary disagreement, and why does safety come first?

blocks.title: Scenario E — A community sports group

blocks.text: A newcomer wants to join a local sports team but worries about not fitting in. The organizer explains expectations kindly, allows the person to observe initially, and provides an accessible way to ask questions. Discussion: How does a welcoming environment strengthen belonging?

On paper, draw three circles labelled “People I trust,” “Places or groups I may choose,” and “Professional services if needed.” Add only contacts you genuinely consider safe. Do not include identifying information if someone else may see the page. A blank circle is not a failure; it identifies a possible area to build gradually.

Choose a low-risk, realistic action: send a greeting, attend one community activity, sit with a classmate at lunch, or reconnect with a trustworthy acquaintance. Afterward, note how comfortable it felt, whether the interaction was respectful, and whether you want to repeat it. Stop or adapt the exercise if it increases distress or risk.

With a willing and trusted partner, take turns speaking about a neutral topic for two minutes. The listener does not interrupt and asks one clarifying question. Then switch roles. Reflect on the difference between listening and immediately solving a problem. Do not use sensitive trauma disclosures for this exercise.

Write a simple statement that describes a limit without blaming another person: “I need some time before discussing this” or “I prefer not to share my account password.” You do not need to deliver it to someone if that would be unsafe.

Think of a school club, sports group, or community event. Ask: Can people attend with limited money or transport? Are newcomers welcomed? Can someone leave without pressure? Are disability needs considered? Is private information protected? Identify one change that could make the activity safer and more inclusive.

items.question: 1. Can a person feel lonely despite having many social contacts?
items.answer: Yes. Loneliness is about perceived unmet connection needs, not only the number of contacts.

items.question: 2. Are solitude and loneliness identical?
items.answer: No. Solitude may be chosen and restorative, while loneliness involves distress.

items.question: 3. Name two elements of a healthy relationship.
items.answer: Examples: respect, trust, boundaries, mutuality, support, or repair after mistakes.

items.question: 4. What is one example of practical social support?
items.answer: Help with transportation, childcare, or completing a necessary task.

items.question: 5. What does active listening involve?
items.answer: Attention, respectful questions, reflection, and not interrupting unnecessarily.

items.question: 6. Does an argument always mean abuse?
items.answer: No. However, threats, coercion, intimidation, or controlling patterns warrant safety attention.

items.question: 7. Is sharing a friend’s personal story online acceptable without asking?
items.answer: No. Seek informed permission and respect privacy.

items.question: 8. Must someone attend large social gatherings to be mentally healthy?
items.answer: No. Connection needs and preferences vary.

items.question: 9. What should you do if setting a boundary could trigger danger?
items.answer: Prioritise safety and seek appropriate professional or specialist guidance.

items.question: 10. When might loneliness warrant professional support?
items.answer: When persistent or accompanied by significant distress, impaired functioning, or other concerning symptoms.

items: Supportive relationships contribute to wellbeing, but people need different types and amounts of connection.
Loneliness is a feeling; social isolation refers to limited interactions; solitude can be chosen.
Quality, respect, boundaries, and safety matter as much as contact frequency.
Small, repeatable, voluntary social actions may be more useful than pressured participation.
A safe relationship allows disagreement without intimidation or coercion.
Professional care is appropriate when distress persists or functioning is affected.

blocks.text: Social connection: Relationships and interactions considered in terms of structure, support function, and quality.
Loneliness: Distress caused by a perceived gap between desired and existing connections.
Social isolation: Relatively few social relationships or interactions.
Emotional boundary: A limit around emotional availability, disclosure, or personal responsibility.
Active listening: Attentive, respectful listening aimed at understanding rather than immediately judging or fixing.
Coercive control: A pattern of intimidation or restrictions used to dominate another person.
Belonging: Feeling accepted and valued as part of a relationship or group.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health
summary: Learn about development, supportive families and schools, bullying, safeguarding, and age-appropriate care.
author: VUGA NDAKUMVA
frontMatter: VUGA NDAKUMVA | MENTAL HEALTH CONTENT LIBRARY
CHAPTER 10
Child and Adolescent
Mental Health
Understanding development, recognizing distress, building supportive families and schools, responding to bullying, and finding appropriate care.
Educational draft — version 1.0 | 11 November 2026
For caregivers, young people, educators, community workers, and readers seeking accurate introductory information. Not a diagnosis or a substitute for clinical assessment.

Safety and safeguarding: If a child is in immediate danger, seriously injured, or at imminent risk of self-harm, seek urgent local emergency help. In Rwanda, the government lists 112 for emergency help, 912 for ambulance, and 116 for the child helpline. Verify current availability and follow local child-protection procedures. [R5]
Learning goals and how to use this chapter

Understand how mental wellbeing develops from childhood through adolescence. Recognize broad groups of mental health challenges without using symptom lists as diagnoses. Identify school, family, social and online pressures alongside protective relationships. Practice safe, age-appropriate conversation and coping skills. Know when routine support is insufficient and how to seek professional or urgent help.

This chapter uses fictional Rwanda-relevant scenarios. They are illustrations, not reports of real children. Caregivers and educators should adapt activities to a child’s developmental level, disability, language, privacy needs and preferences. Avoid forcing disclosures.

sections.title: What does child and adolescent mental health mean?

blocks.text: Child mental health includes emotional wellbeing, developing skills to manage feelings, building friendships, learning, and participating in family and school life. Having good mental health does not mean a child is calm or happy every day. Children may feel frustrated, frightened, angry, or sad while still growing in healthy ways. [R1, R2]

Adolescence commonly refers to ages 10–19. It brings rapid physical, cognitive and social changes. Young people increasingly seek autonomy, explore identity, become sensitive to peer relationships and manage growing responsibilities. These changes are important, but they do not always happen at the same speed. [R1]

The World Health Organization estimated in 2025 that approximately one in seven adolescents aged 10–19 lives with a mental health condition worldwide. This is a global estimate—not a Rwanda-specific prevalence figure—and shows why accessible, non-stigmatizing support matters.

Younger children often communicate distress through behaviour, play, sleep, appetite or physical complaints before they can describe complex feelings. They need adults who help name emotions, keep predictable routines and model calm responses. This does not mean every tantrum or fear is a mental illness.

School-age children usually develop more complex friendships and a growing sense of fairness, achievement and belonging. Academic pressure, conflicts, exclusion, family changes and difficulties with learning can affect mood and confidence. Adults can support them by listening and responding with consistent, fair boundaries.

Adolescents may want privacy, independence and greater control over decisions. Respectful family relationships balance this growing autonomy with appropriate safeguarding. A change in interests or desire for time alone can be normal; a persistent decline in functioning or safety requires attention. [R1, R2]

rows: Name feelings; create safety and routines

blocks.text: A child’s mental health is shaped by interacting biological, psychological and social factors. Family instability, discrimination, food insecurity, chronic illness, harmful punishment, abuse, bullying, isolation or major loss can increase risk. These experiences do not guarantee a disorder, and no single factor explains an individual child’s difficulties. [R1, R3]

Protective factors include caring, dependable adults; safe learning environments; accessible healthcare; friends and community support; opportunities for play and activity; respectful discipline; and skills such as problem-solving and emotional regulation. Protection is a shared responsibility, not a task for the child alone. [R3, R4]

Anxiety and fear: Children may experience persistent worries, fear of separation, social situations or particular events. When fear is intense, prolonged, and interferes with attendance, sleep, relationships or daily activities, assessment may help.

Depression and low mood: Signs may include sustained sadness or irritability, reduced interest, hopelessness, withdrawal or changes in energy and sleep. Irritability in adolescents can be prominent; it should not simply be dismissed as “bad behaviour.”

Attention, behaviour and learning: Persistent attention difficulties, impulsivity, aggression, or school struggles can have different explanations, including neurodevelopmental needs, learning barriers, stress, trauma or sleep problems. Effective responses begin with careful assessment, not punishment.

Trauma, eating concerns and substance use: Some young people experience distress after frightening events, changes in eating or body image, or harmful use of substances. Each deserves sensitive, age-appropriate support and clinical evaluation when needed. [R1, R2]

sections.title: What is a warning sign rather than a normal phase?

blocks.text: A single bad day, argument or lower grade usually does not establish a mental health condition. Pay attention to duration, intensity, change from the child’s usual behaviour, distress and impact on daily life. Persistent school refusal, marked withdrawal, severe sleep changes, repeated unexplained physical complaints, loss of enjoyable activities or significant impairment merit a supportive conversation and possible assessment.

Watch urgently for expressed wishes to die, suicidal behaviour, self-injury, extreme confusion, psychotic symptoms, immediate danger, severe inability to care for basic needs, or signs of abuse. Never wait for a routine appointment if danger appears imminent. [R1, R2]

Do not label or diagnose: “This child has depression” or “This teenager has ADHD” should not follow from a web checklist. Document observations without judgement and consult an appropriately qualified clinician.

School can be a powerful place of belonging, but also a source of distress. Examinations, performance expectations, classroom humiliation, learning differences, peer exclusion and disciplinary practices can influence emotions and participation. Educators can improve wellbeing by building predictable routines, demonstrating fairness, welcoming differences and providing ways to ask for help.

When a learner struggles, private and respectful inquiry is preferable to public embarrassment. Teachers should record observable changes, involve safeguarding or student-support staff according to school procedures, work with caregivers where safe and appropriate, and help families access professional assessment when indicated. [R4]

Bullying generally involves repeated aggression and a power imbalance; it may involve physical acts, insults, humiliation, exclusion, threats or online abuse. Even a single serious incident can require protection. Adults should take reports seriously, make a proportionate safety plan, avoid blaming the affected child, and investigate according to safeguarding procedures.

Online spaces may expose young people to harassment, unwanted sharing of private information, image-based abuse or coercion. Do not require a child to confront an aggressor. Before blocking accounts, collecting screenshots or altering devices, consider whether a harmful person monitors the child’s device and whether a safer adult or professional should assist. [R1, R4]

Children benefit from warmth and consistent boundaries. Caregivers can listen first, acknowledge feelings, explain expectations without threats, offer manageable choices and repair relationships after conflict. “You seem quieter recently; would you like to tell me what has been difficult?” is more inviting than an accusation.

Caregivers should avoid calling children weak, lazy or attention-seeking because of emotional difficulties. Encourage regular sleep opportunities, balanced meals where possible, play, movement, trusted friendships and reasonable schedules without making lifestyle changes the only response to a serious problem.
If a parent or caregiver is the source of harm, the child needs an alternative safe adult and the appropriate safeguarding route—not forced family reconciliation. [R3, R4]

sections.title: Communication that helps young people speak

blocks.text: Choose a private, calm time. Use open questions, listen without interrupting and reflect what you hear. The goal is not to extract a complete story immediately. Ask what feels safest or most helpful right now. A child can decline to answer an optional educational question, and a teenager’s privacy deserves respect within child-protection responsibilities.

Adults should explain confidentiality honestly: they will respect privacy as much as possible, but may need to involve safeguarding or emergency services if someone is in danger or law requires action. Do not promise to keep abuse or immediate danger secret. [R4, R6]

sections.title: Helping a young person experiencing distress

blocks.text: First check immediate safety and basic needs. Offer calm company and validate feelings without assuming a diagnosis. Ask whether they would prefer a different trusted adult, school staff member or health professional. Make a small plan together: who to contact, a suitable time and place, and how to manage school or home demands while support is arranged.

When a child discloses violence or exploitation, do not question them repeatedly, demand evidence, suggest blame or confront the suspected person. Follow child safeguarding procedures and involve trained professionals. The child’s safety and developmental needs take priority. [R4, R6]

sections.title: Mental health in digitally connected lives

blocks.text: Digital experiences can support friendship, learning and peer connection, but may also involve social comparison, disrupted sleep, unwanted contact, harassment or exposure to distressing content. Ask what the young person experiences online instead of assuming all screen time has the same effects. Agree on age-appropriate privacy, bedtime and safety practices. Adults should model respectful online behaviour and avoid secretive surveillance when a collaborative, safer approach is possible. If there is a credible threat, exploitation or urgent safety risk, safeguarding needs may override ordinary privacy expectations.

Children with disabilities, neurodevelopmental differences, chronic illnesses, learning difficulties, displacement histories or experiences of discrimination may face additional barriers to care. Avoid assuming that all distress reflects an existing diagnosis or disability.

Adapt communication by offering simple language, visual supports, extra response time, private alternatives to public sharing, and an accessible route to care. Ask families and young people what accommodations work for them. [R1, R2]

A clinician may speak with the child, caregivers and relevant educators, with appropriate privacy and consent procedures, to understand symptoms, context, functioning, medical history and safety concerns. Care may involve psychological interventions, family support, school adjustments, targeted services or medication when clinically indicated.

WHO recommends evidence-informed psychosocial interventions that build social-emotional skills and prevent mental health problems among adolescents. These are not substitutes for clinical treatment when a condition requires it. Do not recommend medicines, stop existing treatment or conduct trauma-processing therapies through self-help content. [R3]

sections.title: When and how to seek help in Rwanda

blocks.text: For non-emergency concerns, start with a qualified health professional, appropriate local health centre or hospital, and ask about child or adolescent mental health referral options. The Ministry of Health’s Kigali Mental Health Referral Centre publicly lists child and adolescent services; its published contact numbers are +250 793 902 059 and +250 736 440 666. Check current hours, service eligibility and referral arrangements before relying on them. [R7]

For immediate danger or imminent self-harm risk, seek urgent medical or emergency assistance. Rwanda’s government emergency directory lists 112 for emergency assistance, 912 for ambulance and 116 for its child helpline. These are published numbers, not a guarantee that each line is staffed or suitable for every case at every moment. [R5]
Situation: A 15-year-old in secondary school has trouble sleeping before national examinations, avoids friends and fears disappointing family.

Supportive response: A trusted teacher listens privately and checks functioning and safety. Caregivers reduce shaming and help organize realistic preparation and support. If distress persists or worsens, arrange professional assessment.
Situation: A 9-year-old stops joining games after a family move and becomes unusually tearful at school.
Supportive response: Adults ask gently about the transition, restore predictable routines, help build connections and monitor whether symptoms persist or impair daily life.
Situation: A 13-year-old repeatedly avoids school after peers mock their speech in class and online.
Supportive response: School staff address the bullying under safeguarding procedures; the child is not required to confront peers. Adults plan safety and supportive educational adjustments.
Situation: A 16-year-old has become anxious after receiving threatening messages through a shared phone.
Supportive response: A trusted adult checks whether the phone is monitored, considers safe documentation and reporting, and helps the teenager access appropriate support without blaming them.
Situation: A caregiver notices their 17-year-old has lost interest in football and frequently says they feel hopeless.
Supportive response: The caregiver listens, asks directly and calmly about safety, and arranges professional assessment promptly. If there is immediate danger, seek urgent help.
How to practice: Invite the child to choose words or drawings describing a feeling from today. Ask what helped and whether they want to share more. Do not score feelings as right or wrong.
Safety note: Optional; no forced disclosure or public sharing.
How to practice: On paper, write or draw up to three people or services the learner could approach if worried. Include a backup if the first person is unavailable.
Safety note: Do not list a person who may be unsafe; respect a child who cannot name anyone and help identify safe services.
How to practice: Make two columns: “What is worrying me?” and “One safe, manageable next action.” Choose only one low-risk next step.
Safety note: Do not use this exercise to solve situations of abuse through self-reliance.
How to practice: One adult rehearses a supportive opening sentence, one open-ended question, and one nonjudgmental reflection. Then switch roles.
Safety note: Do not dramatize an actual child’s confidential disclosure.
How to practice: Educators review one classroom practice: participation options, respectful correction, anti-bullying responses, and referral routes. Identify a realistic improvement.
Safety note: Follow school safeguarding policies; record no identifying child details in training materials.

sections.title: Knowledge check: questions and explained answers

items.question: 1. Does every emotional change in adolescence indicate a disorder?
items.answer: No. Consider persistence, severity, changes from usual behaviour and effects on everyday functioning.

items.question: 2. What is a protective factor?
items.answer: A condition that supports wellbeing, such as a dependable adult, safer school or accessible care.

items.question: 3. Should a teacher publicly challenge a distressed learner to explain?
items.answer: No. Provide a private, respectful opportunity and follow safeguarding procedures.

items.question: 4. Can bullying affect school attendance and mental health?
items.answer: Yes. Safety and support matter, and repeated power-imbalanced aggression requires attention.

items.question: 5. Is a symptom checklist enough to diagnose ADHD or depression?
items.answer: No. Assessment considers context, history, functioning and alternative explanations.

items.question: 6. What should adults say about confidentiality?
items.answer: Explain privacy respectfully and clarify safeguarding and safety-related limits.

items.question: 7. Should survivors be forced to repeat traumatic disclosures?
items.answer: No. Listen calmly, avoid unnecessary questioning and connect to trained support.

items.question: 8. Can all sleep and mood difficulties be managed only with routines?
items.answer: No. Persistent or severe problems may require professional assessment and treatment.

items.question: 9. What makes digital-safety decisions complicated?
items.answer: Monitoring by a harmful person can make blocking or changing settings risky.

items.question: 10. What happens if there is immediate risk of self-harm?
items.answer: Seek urgent local emergency or medical support; do not rely on an ordinary appointment.

blocks.text: Mental wellbeing: The emotional, psychological and social functioning that supports daily life.
Co-regulation: An adult helping a child manage overwhelming emotions through calm, attuned support.
Protective factor: A condition or resource associated with safer development and resilience.
Bullying: Repeated aggression involving a power imbalance.
Safeguarding: Actions to protect children from harm and respond appropriately to safety concerns.
Psychosocial intervention: Structured support addressing thoughts, behaviour, relationships or social circumstances.
Referral: Connecting someone to a service qualified to assess or provide needed support.
